## 1. Summary
This code shows how to download and pre-process Copernicus High Resolution Layer (HRL) Imperiousness data to compile the URGR indicators from ecRxiv: https://github.com/NINAnor/ecRxiv/tree/main/indicators/NO_URGR_001-005.


## 2. Data characteristics

These data are produced by Copernicus: https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/high-resolution-layer-imperviousness.

### 2.1 Spatial and temporal resolution and extent

We downloaded the data for the whole on Norway (excluding Svalbård), for the years 2018, 2021, and 2024. Spatial resolution is 10m x 10m.

### 2.2 Sampling design
The HRL Imperviousness data are generated using state-of-the-art automated image processing 
methods that are applied to systematically acquired, high-resolution satellite image time series 
from the Copernicus space segment (i.e. Sentinel-2). See [Algorithm Teoretical Basis Document](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/technical-library/algorithm-theoretical-basis-document-high-resolution-layer-imperviousness-2024/@@download/file).

There has been significant changes is data processing between 2018, 2021 and 2024. First, 2021 and 2024 layers have been merged with CLC+ BackBone sealed layer. This ensures comparability between the two Copernicus products. Copernicus IMD 2018 however has not be merged with CLC+ BackBone sealed layer. Years 2021 and 2024 have been produced with the same convolutional neural network called U-Net, while the model used for 2018 is not specified in the metadata but is stated as being different. Finally, the threshold of prediction for an imperviousness density to be reported in a pixel was 90% in 2021 but 70% in 2024. This means that care should be taken when using these data for temporal series analyses. To ensure consistency across time, it would have been preferable to use the Imperviousness change layers that are designed to be homogeneous over time, correcting for the different changes in methodology. However, these layers are only available at 20m resolution. Downscaling theses layers to 10m or upscaling the original layers of HRL Imperviousness to 20m would results in additional uncertainties.

### 2.3 Original units
The original unit of Copernicus HRL imperviousness is percentages (the share of impervious areas in the pixel)


### 2.4 Instructions for citing, using and accessing data
Openly available[here](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/high-resolution-layer-imperviousness/imperviousness-density-2024#download)


### 2.5 Additional comments about the dataset
Other metadata can be found in the [User manual](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/technical-library/product-user-manual-high-resolution-layer-imperviousness-2024/@@download/file)


## 3. Uncertainties
### 3.1 General uncertainties
Uncertainties have several sources all taking roots in the modelling used to process the Sentinel-d raw data. They can come from the pre-processing of the raw data necessary to correct the images (e.g., radiometrical/sensor calibration; geophysical corrections; cloud cover corrections;creation of the mosaic). But they also arise when the pre-processed data are classified through machine learning to produce the final layer of imperviousness. Classification is never definitive and produces probabilities for a pixel to belong to a specific class. In addition, there has been significant methodology changes between the 3 years downloaded: 2018, 2021, and 2024. Care should be taken when comparing imperviousness across years.

### 3.2 Reported uncertainties
Copernicus reported "Confidence layers" for each of the Imperviousness datasets. In their technical guide, they explain that, to compile this indicator of uncertainty, the U-Net classification model is applied multiple times using different models from nearby tiles. The resulting standard deviation of the predictions is used as an indicator for the classification of confidence per pixel.

The confidence values are pixel-based and range from 0 to 100. In practice only values 50-100 are used as values below 50% would indicate a higher confidence in the opposite class. The recommended interpretation state that pixels with values ranging 75-100 are of high confidence, 50-75 of moderate confidence, and below 50 of low confidence.

The confidence layers were only available for 2021 and 2024.


## 4. Data download

### 4.1 Copernicus IMD
Tree canopy cover density layers can be downloaded from Copernicus for the years 2018 to 2023. This can be done using an API query through the [WEkEO website](https://help.wekeo.eu/en/articles/6416936-how-to-download-wekeo-data#h_4d7de19c7c) and the `hda` R package. A detailed tutorial can be found [here](https://help.wekeo.eu/en/articles/7035318-how-to-use-the-hdar-package-for-accessing-the-wekeo-hda-api-in-r).Note that the request through API requires the username and password from the WEkEO website so you nee dto create an account. The API query uses a bounding box but it is quite large, resulting in heavy rasters. That is why a subsequent step of cleaning has been done to mask the cells that were not in Norway, hence decreasing the size of the rasters. These processed rasters are the ones we made available on the internal NINA repository.

*!Attention: this code, writes the rasters on the disk of the users.*

First we need to set up our WekEO credentials.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Set your WEkEO credentials"

## Download data
# Set credentials and save them in ~/.hdarc for future use
username <- "your_username"
password <-"your_password"
client <- Client$new(username, password, save_credentials = TRUE)

# Initialise Client
client <- Client$new()

# Check authentification
client$get_token() 

# Review and accept Terms & Condition before downloading the data
client$show_terms()
client$terms_and_conditions(term_id = 'all')

```

Now we can create the API query. It can be automatically created for you using the [Expert Data Viewer](https://data.wekeo.copernicus.eu/data?view=viewer&objects=W10%3D&). There is an additional trick for HRL TCD though. The API format of these layers have changed and the Expert Data Viewer does not reflect this. It is still useful to take the basic API from the Expert Data Viewer and then modify it with the instructions [here](https://help.wekeo.eu/en/articles/15612836-action-required-changes-to-data-access-for-clms-hrl-datasets).

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Create the API query"

# Create API queries
# Note: use the WEkEO Data viewer that will create an automatic API
# Note: Use "SetAOI" to set your bounding box
yrs <- seq(2021, 2024, 3)

api_list <- map(seq_along(yrs), function(i){
  paste0('{
  "dataset_id": "EO:EEA:DAT:HRL:IMP",
  "bbox": [
    4.035020512779106,
    57.619913920878176,
    32.10650033269319,
    71.32500159191206
  ],
  "productType": "Imperviousness Density",
  "resolution": "10m",
  "year": "', yrs[i],
  '",
  "itemsPerPage": 200,
  "startIndex": 0
}')}
) %>% 
  unlist()

```

We use the API query to search and download the data sets of relevance.
```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Search and dowload the data corresponding to the API query"

# Search the datasets
matches <- map(seq_along(api_list), ~ client$search(api_list[.x]))
names(matches) <- yrs

# ID of all the datasets to download
data_id <- map(matches, function(yr) {
  map_dfr(yr$results, ~ tibble(id = .x$id))
})

# Set up the output directory
output_directory <- paste0(str_remove(tempdir(), "Rtmp\\w*"), "IMD_Copernicus")

# Download - co-written by Sylvie Clappe and Jennifer Hansen
walk(matches, function(yr) {
  
 walk(seq_along(yr$results), function(i) {
  
  product_id <- yr$results[[i]]$id
  
  message(
    sprintf(
      "Downloading %s %d/%d: %s",
      str_extract(product_id, "(?<=IMD_S).{4}"),
      i,
      yr$total_count,
      product_id
    )
  )
  
  tryCatch(
    {
      yr$download(output_dir = output_directory,
                  selected_indexes = i,
                  prompt = FALSE) },
    error = function(e) {
      message("Failed: ", product_id)
      message(conditionMessage(e))
    }
  )
  
  Sys.sleep(1) # to avoid hitting API quota
 })
})

# Clean R environment
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), 
                  c("pull",
                    "client")))


```

## 5. Data cleaning and formatting

### 5.1 Copernicus IMD
All the data have been downloaded as `.zip`. We are now going to unzip them. While we do it, we perform additional cleaning and formatting steps. Norway bounding box for which we downloaded the data is quite wide and include a lot of rasters that are in Sweden and Finland, while not overlapping Norway. We apply a mask for Norway to select the relevant rasters. For this we use the administrative boundaries from Geonorge. We also re-classify the raster value of 255 as NaN.

First, we create a mask of Norway.
```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Load the administrative boundaries"

# Call function
source(here::here("src", "functions", "api_geonorge.R"))

# Open duckdb connection
conn_imd <- ddbs_create_conn(dbidr = "tempdir", threads = 5, memory_limit_gb = 10)

# Download data in tempdir
no_data_path <- api_geonorge("https://nedlasting.geonorge.no/api/capabilities/041f1e6e-bdbc-4091-b48f-8a5990f3cc5b", 
                            "john.doe@email.no")

st_layers(no_data_path)

# Read, transform, union and write 
dbExecute(conn_imd, 
            sprintf("
              CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE '%s' AS
              SELECT ST_Transform(
             ST_Union_Agg(ST_MakeValid(SHAPE)),
             'EPSG:25833',
             'EPSG:3035',
             always_xy := true) AS geometry
              FROM ST_Read('%s', layer = '%s')
            ", 
      "norway_bd",
      no_data_path,
      "kommune"))

# Extract dataset
norway_mask <- as_duckspatial_df("norway_bd", conn = conn_imd) %>%
                ddbs_collect() %>%
                st_set_crs(3035) # duckdb doesn't track the change of the CRS in the database so needs to be done manually

# Verify tables are in my duckdb conn_pm database
ddbs_stop_conn(conn_imd)

# Clean the R environment
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), 
                  c("pull",
                    "output_directory",
                    "norway_mask")))

```

Now that the mask is ready, we can unzip the files and clean the rasters.
```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Read the .tif from a zip file"

# Call functions
source(here::here("src", "functions", "list_zip_files.R"))
source(here::here("src", "functions", "extract_zip_files.R"))


# List datasets' paths to read and their names
files_imd_read <- files_list_one_fn(output_directory)

# List datasets path (here we remove the zip marker and the name of the file)
files_imd_write <- str_remove(files_imd_read[[1]], "CLMS.*") %>%
                      str_remove("/vsizip/\\{")

# Run the function to read and write the rasters from the zip files directly
daemons(10)
map(seq_along(files_imd_read[[1]]),
    in_parallel( ~process_raster_fn(path_read = files_imd_read[[1]][.x],
                                    path_write = files_imd_write[.x],
                                    files_names = files_imd_read[[2]][.x],
                                    geo_mask = norway_mask),
                 process_raster_fn = process_raster_fn,
                 files_imd_read = files_imd_read,
                 files_imd_write = files_imd_write,
                 norway_mask = norway_mask
    )
)

daemons(0)

# Clean the R environment
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), 
                  c("pull",
                    "output_directory")))

```


We now create a virtual raster that we will read and export as a raster for future analyses. These rasters are not heavy (<2GB each).

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Create Copernicus IMD virtual rasters and export them as rasters"

## Code co-created by Sylvie Clappe and Jennifer Hansen

## Create the IMD virtual rasters
output_directory <- "~/Mounts/P-Prosjekter2/412413_2023_no_egd/git_data/IMD_Copernicus/IMD_10m_2018"
file_imd_list <- dir(output_directory, recursive = FALSE, pattern = ".tif$", full.names = TRUE)
yrs_imd <- str_extract(file_imd_list, "(?<=IMD_S).{4}") %>%
              unique()

output_directory <- paste0(str_remove(tempdir(), "Rtmp\\w*"), "IMD_Copernicus")

file_imd <- map_vec(seq_along(yrs_imd), function(i){paste0(output_directory, "/IMD_", yrs_imd[i], ".vrt")})

walk(seq_along(file_imd), function(x){
  
  # Select relevant .tif
    file_imd_list[grepl(yrs_imd[x], file_imd_list, ignore.case = TRUE)] %>%
    
  # Create virtual raster
    vrt(filename= file_imd[x]) } )
               
        
## Read .vrt files
rast_list <- map(seq_along(file_imd),
                 ~rast(file_imd[.x]))

## Create levels (none in the original datset)
levels_original <- data.frame(value = c(seq(0, 100), 255),
                              class_name = c(paste0(0:100, "% imperviousness"),
                              "outside area reclassified as NAs"))

rast_list <- map(rast_list,
                 ~{levels(.x) <- levels_original
                 return(.x)})

## Export new rasters
walk(seq_along(file_imd),
     ~writeRaster(rast_list[[.x]], filename = paste0(output_directory, "/IMD_", yrs_imd[.x], ".tif")))

```
